Singapore is making parenthood cheaper to reverse birth rate decline. But baby push has its limits

The package includes thousands of dollars in direct assistance in addition to a S10,000(7,879) “baby gift” and more full-day childcare subsidies.

Philip J. Heijmans ,  Srinidhi Ragavendran  and  Gabrielle Ng

24 August, 2026 02:21 pm IST

Facebook

PM Wong unveils major family support package and plans for Singapore’s future (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Text Size: A- A+

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong’s latest family support package is a familiar strategy for Singapore: make parenthood cheaper and easier in the hope that people will have more children. The record shows there are limits to how much that can actually achieve.

The 53-year-old premier drew applause, and even some oohs and aahs, from the audience Sunday night during his National Day Rally speech, as he unveiled one of the world’s most generous attempts to reverse a record decline in Singapore’s birth rate. The package includes thousands of dollars in direct assistance in addition to a S$10,000 ($7,879) “baby gift” and more full-day childcare subsidies.

For Jason Gan, a 28-year-old business development manager expecting his first child in November, the extra help is welcome. “It’s given me a financial sigh of relief,” said Gan, the first among his friends to become a parent.

Show Full Article

The funds could go toward groceries and enrichment classes, and mean fewer trips across the border to Malaysia for cheaper essentials, but he’s less convinced it will persuade others. It’s good for those “like me that are about to be parents, but I don’t think that’s really the long-term solution here.”

Wong has couched the latest push as a shift away from a traditional reliance on baby incentives, saying in June that the government would focus instead on making family life easier. It’s unclear yet if that can surmount the growing concerns among younger Singaporeans about the rising pressures and perceived constraints of raising children.

Parents often weigh children against the quality of life and freedom they would otherwise enjoy, said Sam Yam, an associate dean at the National University of Singapore’s business school and a professor of psychology and bioethics.

“They don’t mean money in their pocket,” Yam said. He likened the new support for people who already have or are planning children to giving someone a discount for a movie after they already bought the ticket. “In effect, the government is giving everyone at the cinema already a $5 rebate that they never asked for,” he said.

That trade-off resonates with Huang Ying Yi, 24, who said the pressure of Singapore’s education and work culture makes parenthood less appealing.

“Some of us have no desire to birth a child just for it to go through the motions and join the rat race, becoming a cog in the machine,” she said. “You always have to keep up with other people.”

A YouGov survey published days before Wong’s speech found nearly one-third of Singaporeans aged 18 to 44 said no government policy would make them more willing to have children, while lower-cost preschool and childcare ranked highest among measures that could encourage parenthood.

With declining birth rates threatening to compound over generations, the latest measures may be “Singapore’s last opportunity to get it right,” said Eugene Tan, an associate professor of law at the Singapore Management University. “Whether they will work will depend on social norms and mindsets being accommodative of marriage and parenthood,” he said.

For a small but wealthy nation where citizens make up just 60% of the 6.1 million population, a total fertility rate that fell to a record low 0.87 last year represents an existential concern, especially as it’s on course to be a “super-aged” society. The problem is hardly unique to Singapore.

China’s birth rate dropped to its lowest on record last year, while Japan’s fertility rate also fell to a fresh low. In May, Taiwan announced plans to launch government-subsidized investment accounts for people between six and 18 years old to reverse its plummeting birth rate.

South Korea’s fertility rate has inched up for a second year — yet only to 0.8 — as marriages show signs of recovery after a prolonged slump, supported by incentives designed to ease the financial burden of raising children.

To help incentivize more children, Singapore is now aiming to underwrite almost the entirety of childhood, not just the first moments. Every Singaporean newborn will receive S$2,000 in child credits annually, a S$5,000 “first step” grant and thousands more as the years go on — in addition to the baby gift. The number of parental leave days was expanded as well.

All-in, each child will receive almost S$70,000 in direct assistance through age 17. The biggest pop from the crowd Sunday night came when Wong announced families applying for build-to-order flats will receive an additional ballot for every child they have or are expecting, drastically improving the odds of securing high-demand public housing.

“What we can do is make it easier for Singaporeans who want children to start and raise a family, and we want every family to know: If you choose to have children, the government will stand with you,” he said against a pink backdrop during his remarks at the Institute of Technical Education.

The drive for babies is a far cry from the “Two Is Enough” campaign launched in the early 1970s, when too many children was seen as a drag on the country’s development and resources. Since the city-state reversed course on population policy in 1987, measures have included thousands of dollars in handouts and extended maternity leave.

The government ran matchmaking events for university graduates and a short-lived program that gave children of highly educated mothers priority in primary-school registration if they had three or more children. Then-Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew remarked at the time that women ought not to work “jobs where they cannot, at the same time, be mothers.”

Yet by 2010 and 2011, the birth rate had fallen to its lowest levels in nearly half a century of independence. With rates continuing to drop, the government set up a workgroup to review marriage and parenthood measures and, in February, announced plans to spend nearly S$7 billion on related initiatives this fiscal year.

Even still, Eugene Godfrey Lee, a 32-year-old executive senior financial consultant, said the latest measures may “kickstart the process” of planning for a family. “At the very least, it will let us feel more supported by the country,” he said.

The prime minister acknowledged the limits, saying on Sunday that Singapore would also have to continue welcoming immigrants while ensuring citizens remain the majority.

“All this means that in the coming years, our overall population will grow more slowly, and our labor force will grow more slowly too,” he said.

Indian food safety officer shakes up Mumbai, one viral raid at a time

Reuters

24 August, 2026 08:30 am IST

Facebook

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

By Arpan Chaturvedi, Vibhuti Sharma and Dhwani Pandya MUMBAI, Aug 24 (Reuters) – Tukaram Mundhe is an Indian bureaucrat on a mission.

As a state food safety commissioner, the 51-year-old has raided food businesses in the country’s commercial capital Mumbai in an unprecedented crackdown on poor hygiene and unsafe food that has captivated the public nationwide.

Mundhe has led the suspension of food permits of four Domino’s and one Pizza Hut outlet in recent weeks, and has also targeted cricket clubs, hotels and well-known restaurants in over 3,000 raids since he took over as Maharashtra’s food safety chief in May.

Show Full Article

When a Mumbai judge accused Mundhe of selective aggression towards private outlets and asked if court canteens were checked, his teams conducted inspections there within hours, shutting some of them which operated without licenses.

“Those who try to not comply, they will face what is expected from the regulator,” Mundhe said in an interview with Reuters, talking about his no-nonsense approach.

“You are dealing with the lives of people.”

Mundhe has won widespread public admiration across India because he has tapped into deep public frustration. Even though foreign chains such as Domino’s and McDonald’s are fast expanding, it is local eateries, roadside kiosks and small restaurants — long dogged by concerns over hygiene — that remain hugely popular.

Each year since 2020, Indian food inspectors have checked more than 100,000 food samples and found roughly 20% to be unsafe, substandard or lacking proper labels, government data shows. Nearly 8,000 food business licenses have been cancelled in the last three years.

“Everyone has tried to normalise this for years by saying it happens in India. It’s basically bottled-up anger,” said Ankur Bisen, a partner at consumer consulting firm The Knowledge Company.

“I have never seen anyone like Mundhe. It’s giving people hope.”

FINDING RATS AND EXPIRED FOOD

Mundhe, who is bespectacled and sports a chevron moustache, has an unconventional operating style.

He has featured in TV interviews declaring nobody dare bribe him, and that he is not afraid of administrative action despite being transferred numerous times in his 21-year career as an officer of the highly regarded Indian Administrative Service. “I get transferred every year,” he said in a 2018 interview.

Now, his food safety team’s actions go viral daily — raids lead to detailed public statements and graphic images that show interiors of eateries and grocery warehouses with stained walls, crawling cockroaches and rats, and even expired food — photos that have shocked many Indians.

“It was surprising. I did not expect these many violations,” Mundhe said.

In Mumbai, Reuters visits last week to 25 street vendors and restaurants showed heightened fear about Mundhe’s raids. One vendor has swapped artificial red dye for natural chilli in Chinese offerings, while another has started changing his frying oil three times a day and requires staff to wear gloves and head caps.

Mumbai’s omnipresent street food ‘vada pav’ — a spicy potato patty in a bun — has not escaped Mundhe’s attention. In June, he prohibited use of newspapers as packaging material — often used to wrap the delicacy.

Customers are noticing the change and consuming street food more confidently. Supriya Wagle, 14, is happy her favourite vada pav is now being packed in cleaner butter paper, saying that is “surely a relief”.

CRITICISM AMID CELEBRITY STATUS

After finding lapses at some Domino’s and Pizza Hut stores, Mundhe’s team on Friday suspended the permit of a McDonald’s outlet after finding “live pest activity (cockroaches)” and “rotting food”. The three companies did not respond to Reuters queries.

Mundhe’s crackdown has included action against a Mumbai British-era cricket club, a 70-year-old ice cream parlour and a 110-year-old Parsi Dairy.

He is facing criticism from businesses that say they should be given time to adapt, with some approaching the High Court and accusing his department of high-handedness.

In one case, the judges fined his department 500,000 rupees ($5,225) for continued suspension of an eatery even though it improved its compliance.

“If there are observations by the court, we take it seriously … if there is scope for improvement, we improve,” Mundhe said.

At an event in New Delhi on Friday, fans clicked quick selfies with Mundhe and jostled to shake his hand. One fan told him Prime Minister Narendra Modi should give him a national role.

“I don’t think I’m a celebrity. I’m just a food safety commissioner,” he told Reuters.

(Editing by Aditya Kalra and Muralikumar Anantharaman)

North Korea preparing further Russia troop deployments, no sign move imminent, Seoul says

Reuters

24 August, 2026 08:00 am IST

Facebook

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

SEOUL, Aug 24 (Reuters) – South Korea’s Defence Ministry said North Korea was continuing preparations for an additional troop deployment to Russia, but had detected no signs that such a deployment was imminent, according to a South Korean lawmaker’s office.

The assessment came after North Korea’s Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, last week denied Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy’s claim that Pyongyang planned to send up to 50,000 more troops to Russia to fight for its ally.

South Korea’s Defence Ministry said in a statement to lawmaker Yu Yong-weon that North Korea had continued to supply Russia with weapons systems, including short-range ballistic missiles, according to Yu’s office.

Show Full Article

North Korea is estimated to have supplied Russia with more than 15 million rounds of artillery ammunition, measured in 152-millimetre shell equivalents, it said.

The lawmaker’s office, citing a South Korean Defense Intelligence Agency assessment, said North Korean missiles used in the war may have improved in accuracy through battlefield data, alongside Russian technical advice and component support.

The ministry also said the development of some North Korean ballistic missiles and multiple rocket launchers assessed as being intended for use in a conflict with South Korea was nearing completion, the lawmaker’s office said.

The ministry added that North Korea’s Hwasong-12 intermediate-range ballistic missile, capable of reaching the U.S. territory of Guam, was being prepared for operational deployment, according to Yu’s office.

North Korea’s intercontinental ballistic missiles have the flight capability to reach the U.S. mainland, the ministry said, but key technologies, including warhead re-entry, have not been verified because all test launches have been conducted on lofted trajectories.

North Korea and Russia have deepened military cooperation since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, with Pyongyang supplying artillery ammunition and missiles since 2023 and deploying troops from 2024, according to South Korean, Ukrainian and Western assessments.

Moscow and Pyongyang have previously denied arms transfers.

(Reporting by Joyce LeeEditing by Ed Davies)

Man suspected of murdering five in Oregon found dead

Reuters

24 August, 2026 08:00 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Aug 23 (Reuters) – A man suspected of killing five people in rural Oregon was found dead in a suspected suicide, local law enforcement said on Sunday.

• The deceased individuals were found on Saturday at a home in a rural community near Forest Grove, Oregon, around 30 miles (48 km) outside Portland, when authorities responded to a report of a vehicle fire.

• An unspecified number of domesticated animals were also found deceased at the home, authorities said.

Show Full Article

• “In my 22 years here, I have not been a part of or witnessed a scene quite this complex,” said Caprice Massey, the sheriff in Washington County, Oregon, where the alleged killings occurred.

• The Washington County Sheriff’s Office identified 36-year-old Benjamin Charles Parker as the suspect. Local police found Parker dead in his vehicle in Enumclaw, Washington, around 45 miles outside Seattle. He is believed to have died by suicide, they said.

(Reporting by Jody Godoy in New York; Editing by Christian Schmollinger)
